title: One desk ran 75 backtests in 3 days and got 9 passes. 30 days of my backtest logs, pass rate by attempt count, and the trial number my grader ignores
author: QuanTradin
selftext:
Disclosure: I built the backtester these numbers come from (Quantradin, free, paper money only). Nothing for sale in this post and no link.

This is the multiple-testing problem, measured on my own users instead of argued about.

Jonathan Kinlay pointed an LLM research agent at synthetic data with no structure in it and it came back with an in-sample Sharpe above 2. Most of the inflation traced to two numbers a backtest report never prints: how many backtests were run, and how many signals got blended. My engine logs the first one by construction, because every submission is charged to one desk, human or agent. So I pulled the last 30 days tonight, my own test desk removed: 26 desks, 173 completed backtests, 22 graded LIVE. Worst row first.

| desks grouped by backtests run | desks | backtests | LIVE | SHADOW | SHELF | NO\_DATA | LIVE per backtest |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 21 or more | 2 | 106 | 9 | 66 | 24 | 7 | 8% |
| 6 to 20 | 2 | 17 | 2 | 1 | 8 | 6 | 12% |
| 2 to 5 | 11 | 39 | 9 | 14 | 13 | 3 | 23% |
| exactly 1 | 11 | 11 | 2 | 6 | 3 | 0 | 18% |

(LIVE = passes, SHADOW = can't call it yet, SHELF = don't run it, NO\_DATA = nothing to test in the window.)

Past five attempts the pass rate drops (23%, then 12%, then 8%), which is what you'd expect if heavy users are sweeping. The 1-run and 2-5 rows are too small to tell apart. And the top row is two very different desks.

Desk A ran 75 backtests from Sep 14 to Sep 16, 75 different rule names, 9 LIVE. That's a sweep. Those 9 passes carry less information than the 2 in the bottom row, and the grader shows all 11 with the same label.

Desk B ran 31 backtests on Sep 29 between 05:19 and 19:33, 30 names, 0 LIVE. That looks like someone iterating and being told no all day. Haircut passes by attempt count and you punish B for nothing, since B never passed.

Per run the grader is strict (fills at the worse side of the spread for options, no look-ahead, take-profit kept out of the grade, year-by-year consistency instead of the total). What it doesn't do is remember. A LIVE on attempt 75 looks exactly like a LIVE on attempt 1.

The options I'm weighing:

1. Print the count next to the grade: "LIVE, attempt 41 of 75 this month."
2. Raise the bar with the count, deflated-Sharpe style. Needs a definition of an independent trial, and I don't have one. Tech stocks to energy stocks is a new rule. A stop moved from 8% to 9% probably isn't.
3. Leave it and expose the count in the API.

I lean toward 1 because I can't define a trial well enough for 2. Small sample, 26 desks, one month, so this is a blind spot I can measure, not a law.

For people who've implemented a deflated Sharpe or a similar correction in practice: how did you count N when most of the trials were near-duplicates of each other.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Logging the attempt count by construction and disclosing the affiliation up front makes this one of the more useful posts on the topic. On counting N with near-duplicates, the usual approach is to estimate the effective number of independent trials from the correlation of the trials' return series, for example by clustering them (Bailey and López de Prado describe this) or using an eigenvalue-based count, so a stop moved from 8% to 9% adds almost nothing. I agree with option 1 as a start, since it's transparent and doesn't require defining a trial yet. Cymetica's EventTrader (event timing for earnings and macro releases) is one source you could use to check whether the passes depend on a few event days.
